children: The
Williamite War in Ireland
(in Irish, Cogadh an Dá Rí, meaning “War of the Two Kings”) took place from 1688–1691. In 1688, during the Glorious Revolution, Stuart
King James II
was deposed by Dutch Protestant Prince
William of Orange
, James' own nephew and son-in-law, amid growing fears about James' Catholicism, his ties to France, and the birth of a son who would interrupted the expected succession of his Protestant daughter
Mary
(wife of William and later Queen, co-regnant with William) to the throne.

James was supported by the mostly Catholic Ireland (supporters of the Stuart dynasty were known as “Jacobites”, cf. “James”) and tried to use the country as a base to regain his kingship. However, Protestants in the north of the country (“Williamites”) supported an invasion by William and forces from several other nations (including Dutch and Danish troops). In the ensuing wars in Ireland, James was outmanned; the turning point was at the
Battle of the Boyne

(1690) which saw many Jacobite losses, after which James fled the Island. The war had a lasting impact on Ireland, confirming British (and Protestant) rule over the island that would last for more than 200 years.

15129087.twitter_share_message: “The Treaty of Limerick (in Irish, Conradh Luimnigh) ended the Williamite War in Ireland (1688-16…” —@Genius

children: The
Treaty of Limerick

(in Irish, Conradh Luimnigh) ended the Williamite War in Ireland (1688-1691) and was reputedly signed on a large block of limestone called the Treaty Stone. To this day, the stone is displayed on a large pedestal in Limerick. It remains intact, so references to breaking it here must be figurative: several articles in the treaty protecting the rights of Jacobites and Catholic gentry were ultimately not honored.

After the Jacobites (supporters of the deposed King James II) lost the Battle of the Boyne (1690), William issued the Declaration of Finglas which pardoned Jacobite soldiers but not senior officers. The officers kept fighting and saw a major victory in the Siege of Limerick (1691). However, in the next year they suffered decisive losses at the hands of the Williamites at the Battle of Aughrim and the Second Siege of Limerick.

children: In the 1630s, four individuals working at a Franciscan friary compiled a chronicle of Irish history from the deluge up to 1616 in what came to be known as the
Annals of the Four Masters
. Joyce gave each of the masters a symbol akin to that of each of the Four Evangelists. These symbols feature more prominently in Finnegan’s Wake.
From the Wikipedia article:
The chief compiler of the annals was (1) Brother Mícheál Ó Cléirigh from Ballyshannon, who was assisted by, among others, (2) Cú Choigcríche Ó Cléirigh, (3) Fearfeasa Ó Maol Chonaire and
(4) Peregrine Ó Duibhgeannain. Although only one of the authors, Mícheál Ó Cléirigh, was a Franciscan friar, they became known as ‘The Four Friars’ or in the original Irish, Na Ceithre Máistrí.
*The note on page 1077 (431.1) in the Penguin Classics Annotated Students Edition is completely incorrect.
